title: Episode 79: What Comes Next
description: How to continue learning, contributing, and building confidence after the workshop.
concepts: How to keep practicing without the live workshop structure
Turning workshop evidence into a portfolio story
Continuing with GitHub Skills and Community Access resources
Building a sustainable open source habit
transcriptText:
﻿[ALEX]
Welcome back. You made it to the end of the workshop, and this conversation is really about graduation in the practical sense: what you accomplished, what it proves, where to go next, and how to keep building from here.

[JAMIE]
I like that framing, because a lot of learners finish something and immediately think, "Okay, but am I actually ready for anything real?"

[ALEX]
Yes, and the answer here is not, "You memorized some terms." It is, "You did real work." You set up a GitHub account, configured accessibility settings, used repositories, filed issues, opened pull requests, responded to automated feedback, resolved conflicts, reviewed code, explored labels and boards, and managed notifications.

[JAMIE]
So day one was not just clicking around. It was learning to function inside GitHub as a contributor.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And then locally, in VS Code and the terminal, you installed and configured your editor with accessibility settings, cloned a repository, worked with Git on your machine, learned the mental model of working directory, staging area, and repository, then created branches, staged changes, committed, and pushed from the command line.

[JAMIE]
And that mental model matters because once you understand where changes live, Git gets much less mysterious.

[ALEX]
Right. You also explored GitHub Copilot, including suggestions, chat, and code review. You created an issue template. You used the fork-based open source workflow. You explored accessibility agents. And you completed a capstone path by designing or improving an agentic asset for Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another repository.

[JAMIE]
That is a lot. And I want to underline something the source makes very clear: this is not just what you were taught. It is what you actually did.

[ALEX]
Yes. That distinction matters. The evidence is on your GitHub profile now: issues filed, pull requests merged, code reviews completed, and capstone evidence prepared for a real repository. Not a certificate. A commit history.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let me ask the nervous learner question. What skills do I actually have now, in a way that transfers beyond this workshop?

[ALEX]
A strong set. Repository navigation transfers to basically every GitHub project and every job that uses GitHub. Issue tracking applies to bug reports, feature requests, and project management. Pull request workflow applies to contribution at companies and in open source. Merge conflict resolution applies anywhere multiple people touch the same code or content.

[JAMIE]
And Git fundamentals are obviously broader than one repo.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Git fundamentals carry into nearly every software project using version control. VS Code proficiency transfers into daily development work in many languages. Code review supports peer review, quality assurance, and collaboration. Fork workflow is essential for open source and often useful in cross-team work. AI-assisted development skills transfer to Copilot, agents, and whatever new tools arrive next. And accessibility awareness applies everywhere if you want to build inclusive software and meet accessibility expectations like WCAG.

[JAMIE]
I also appreciated the section about skills learners may not even notice they practiced.

[ALEX]
Those are some of the most important ones. First, reading documentation. You navigated technical guides, followed written instructions, and used references to troubleshoot. That is a core developer skill, maybe the core developer skill. Second, asking for help effectively. You learned to include context, error messages, and what you already tried. That is how experienced developers communicate. Third, learning tools by doing. You did not wait to master every manual before acting. You experimented, got stuck, adjusted, and continued. That is real tool learning.

[JAMIE]
So if someone says, "I still feel like a beginner," the response is, "Sure, but now you are a beginner with real workflow skills."

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay. If GitHub activity is now evidence, how do learners turn that into a portfolio people can actually understand?

[ALEX]
Start with your GitHub profile, because that is your portfolio. One concrete step is to pin your best repositories. Go to your profile settings, then the pinned repositories area, and choose projects that show meaningful work.

[JAMIE]
What kinds of repos should be pinned?

[ALEX]
A strong choice would be your fork of the accessibility-agents repository because it demonstrates open source contribution. Then add personal projects you build after the workshop. The key is to showcase work that tells a story about your interests and capabilities.

[JAMIE]
And then there is the profile README, which is such a useful feature.

[ALEX]
Very useful. You create a repository with exactly the same name as your username, and add a README.md. That README becomes a front-page introduction. A simple structure works well: a greeting with your name, a short sentence about what you focus on, a recent work section, and a what-I-am-learning section.

[JAMIE]
So something like: I am a developer focused on accessibility, open source, or AI-assisted workflows, then a few bullets about workshop completion and capstone work, then a short list of technologies or ideas you are exploring next.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Keep it honest and current. You do not need to sound impressive. You need to sound real.

[JAMIE]
And there is also the contribution graph, which people talk about a lot.

[ALEX]
Yes. The contribution graph shows your activity over time. Small actions count: filing issues, opening pull requests, making commits, reviewing code. The important idea is consistency over volume. A steady pattern of engagement says more than one giant burst followed by silence.

[JAMIE]
I want to make sure we include the learning-card accessibility guidance here, because that is part of the material, not optional side commentary.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. For screen reader users, the profile settings page includes the pinned repositories section as a group of checkboxes. Tab through and press Space to pin or unpin. The profile README repository name must match your username exactly, including case sensitivity as described in the source. When visitors navigate your profile, screen readers will read the rendered README as regular page content. And the contribution graph is typically announced as a table or grid, where arrow keys move between day cells and each cell announces the date and contribution count.

[JAMIE]
That is especially helpful because the contribution graph can seem very visual if it is not described.

[ALEX]
Right. For low-vision users, pinned repositories appear as cards below your avatar, and at high zoom that grid may reflow into a single column, which can actually improve scanning. Your profile README renders in your current GitHub theme, so test it in both light and dark modes to make sure text and images remain readable. And because the contribution graph uses green intensity to indicate activity, high-contrast mode can help if those shade differences are hard to distinguish.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users?

[ALEX]
Pinned repositories appear prominently below the bio, usually in a two-by-three grid, so visitors see them immediately. The profile README renders above that section, so it should be concise, scannable, and structured with headings and bullets. And the contribution graph shows a year of activity, where steady small contributions usually create a stronger impression than occasional spikes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Once a learner has that portfolio foundation, the next question is usually, "What should I study next?" And I know the roadmap breaks this down by area.

[ALEX]
It does. For Git and version control, a major recommendation is the Pro Git book, which is free, comprehensive, and widely respected. Starting with chapters two and three is a practical path. There is also an advanced Git appendix covering concepts like rebasing, cherry-picking, and stashing, which you do not need immediately but will eventually.

[JAMIE]
So that is the deeper technical layer after the fundamentals.

[ALEX]
Yes. For the GitHub platform itself, bookmark GitHub Docs. That should become a standard reference. GitHub Skills is also recommended because it teaches by doing through interactive courses. And the GitHub Blog helps you stay current on new features and best practices.

[JAMIE]
What about VS Code?

[ALEX]
Go to the official VS Code documentation for settings, keybindings, extensions, and the broader editor model. And for this audience especially, the VS Code accessibility documentation matters: screen reader support, keyboard navigation, high contrast, and related settings.

[JAMIE]
And accessibility as a learning path deserves its own lane.

[ALEX]
Definitely. The workshop points learners toward WCAG 2.2, especially the quick reference, because it is practical. There is also the workshop appendix on accessibility standards, plus resources like WebAIM and Deque University for practical guidance, training, and deeper study.

[JAMIE]
Then the AI-assisted development lane.

[ALEX]
Right. Continue with the official GitHub Copilot documentation for features, configuration, and best practices. Use the workshop's Copilot reference appendix as a quick lookup. And the agents reference appendix gives you the broader accessibility agents roster and command reference.

[JAMIE]
The source also points toward programming languages, even though the visible excerpt cuts off the detailed table.

[ALEX]
Yes, but the key guidance is still clear: choose a language based on your interests. The point is not to chase the one true language. If you are drawn to web work, automation, data, accessibility tooling, or app development, choose accordingly and start where motivation is strongest.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let us talk about GitHub Skills courses specifically. Why are they called out separately?

[ALEX]
Because they are a practical next step inside the GitHub ecosystem. They are free, interactive, and aligned with the same learn-by-doing approach used in the workshop. The recommendation is to use them as structured practice rather than passive reading.

[JAMIE]
Do we know the exact course list from the source excerpt here?

[ALEX]
The excerpt does not preserve the full list, so the safest teaching point is the method: use the recommended next courses in GitHub Skills to reinforce your workflow knowledge, and begin a course directly through the GitHub Skills site. In general, that means choosing a course, starting it in GitHub, and completing the guided tasks in real repositories or sandbox environments.

[JAMIE]
So the skill is not just picking a course. It is knowing how to begin one and treat it like hands-on practice.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Then there is the social side of growth: staying connected.

[ALEX]
Yes. Continued learning is easier when you stay connected to community. The material calls out Community Access, open source contribution, and the accessibility community. The big idea is that you should not disappear after the workshop. Keep reading, participating, and contributing.

[JAMIE]
What might that look like in practice?

[ALEX]
It can mean following projects you care about, watching repositories selectively, participating in discussions, opening issues, responding to other contributors, and staying engaged with accessibility-focused spaces where inclusive design and assistive technology are part of the conversation. It can also mean continuing to contribute to open source through forks, pull requests, issue triage, documentation updates, testing, and reviews.

[JAMIE]
I am glad you mentioned documentation and testing, because learners often assume open source only values code.

[ALEX]
That leads perfectly into contributing back to this workshop.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Yes, because the material explicitly invites learners to contribute back. What kinds of contributions are valued?

[ALEX]
The principle is broad: not just code. Valuable contributions include clarifying instructions, improving accessibility notes, fixing errors, refining examples, improving documentation, and strengthening the learning experience for future participants.

[JAMIE]
And the workflow should feel familiar by now.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The contribution workflow builds on what you already practiced: identify something to improve, likely discuss it through an issue if needed, create a branch or fork depending on the repository permissions, make the change, and open a pull request with clear context. In other words, the workshop is not only something you completed. It is also something you are now qualified to help improve.

[JAMIE]
That is a powerful shift in identity.

[ALEX]
It is. And the learning-card framing matters here too: contributing back is itself another portfolio artifact. It demonstrates that you can improve educational material, collaborate asynchronously, and make tools or content more accessible for the next learner.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
What if someone leaves the workshop excited, then gets stuck a week later and feels embarrassed to ask for help?

[ALEX]
Then I would remind them that getting stuck after the workshop is normal. The right response is the same one you practiced throughout: go to the docs, review your notes and appendices, look at the workshop materials, compare your workflow to known examples, and ask for help with context. Include what you were trying to do, what happened, the exact error if there is one, and what you already attempted.

[JAMIE]
So being stuck is not evidence that you failed. It is evidence that you are still doing the work.

[ALEX]
Precisely.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we close, I want to circle back to something from the very beginning. This lesson is intentionally the final stop in the companion audio path.

[ALEX]
Yes. That matters. You can still use reference episodes and documentation to look up details later. But this moment is for the bigger question: what will you do next with the skills you now have?

[JAMIE]
And maybe one answer is: build in public, even a little. Keep a profile README. Pin meaningful work. Make small contributions. Stay active.

[ALEX]
That is an excellent answer. Another is: keep learning deliberately. Use GitHub Docs. Use GitHub Skills. Use the Pro Git book. Use VS Code documentation. Use the accessibility resources. Use the Copilot and agents references. The source also points you back to related appendices for resources, GitHub Skills, and workshop materials, which means you already have a map.

[JAMIE]
And the authoritative sources behind this whole path include GitHub Skills and GitHub Docs for getting started.

[ALEX]
Yes. Those are dependable places to return to. More broadly, the section-level source map emphasizes GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog and Blog, Git concepts, GitHub flow, and pull request documentation as core references across the chapter. That is a useful signal: your future growth will keep circling back to official docs and real workflow guidance.

[JAMIE]
Final question. If a learner remembers only one thing from this closing conversation, what should it be?

[ALEX]
You are not leaving with abstract exposure. You are leaving with evidence, workflow habits, and a next-step roadmap. You know how to navigate, contribute, collaborate, troubleshoot, and keep learning.

[JAMIE]
And that means the next step does not have to be huge. It just has to be real.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Pin a repo. Write the profile README. Start a GitHub Skills course. Read some docs. Open a small issue. Make a small pull request. Keep going.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Congratulations, truly.

[ALEX]
Congratulations. We are glad you made it here. Now go build what comes next.

# What Comes Next: Your Developer Journey

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix X: Resources](appendix-x-resources.md) | [Appendix Z: GitHub Skills](appendix-z-github-skills.md) | [Appendix Y: Workshop Materials](appendix-y-workshop-materials.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com/) | [GitHub Docs: Getting started](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started)

> **Day 2, Closing Material**
>
> Congratulations -- you have completed the Git Going with GitHub workshop. This chapter is your graduation guide: what you accomplished, where to go next, how to build your portfolio, and how to stay connected with the community.
>
> If you are following the companion audio path, this lesson is intentionally the final stop. Reference episodes may help you look up details, but this chapter brings you back to the bigger question: what will you do next with the skills you now have?

## Table of Contents

1. [What You Built in Two Days](#1-what-you-built-in-two-days)
2. [Your New Skills Inventory](#2-your-new-skills-inventory)
3. [Building Your Developer Portfolio](#3-building-your-developer-portfolio)
4. [Continued Learning Roadmap](#4-continued-learning-roadmap)
5. [GitHub Skills Courses to Try Next](#5-github-skills-courses-to-try-next)
6. [Staying Connected](#6-staying-connected)
7. [Contributing Back to This Workshop](#7-contributing-back-to-this-workshop)
8. [Final Words](#8-final-words)

---

## 1. What You Built in Two Days

Take a moment to appreciate what you accomplished. This is not a list of what you were taught -- it is a list of what you did.

### Day 1: You Can Navigate This

- Created and configured a GitHub account with accessibility settings
- Navigated repositories, files, and folders using your screen reader, keyboard, or preferred tools
- Filed issues with descriptive titles, labels, and context
- Created branches, edited files, and opened pull requests
- Responded to bot feedback and passed automated checks
- Resolved a merge conflict
- Reviewed someone else's code and gave constructive feedback
- Explored labels, milestones, and project boards
- Managed notifications

### Day 2: You Can Build This

- Installed and configured VS Code with accessibility settings
- Cloned a repository and worked with Git locally
- Understood the mental model: working directory, staging area, repository
- Created branches, staged changes, committed, and pushed from the command line
- Explored GitHub Copilot: code suggestions, chat, and code review
- Created an issue template
- Forked a repository and contributed using the open source workflow
- Explored the accessibility agents ecosystem
- Completed a capstone contribution path by designing or improving an agentic asset for Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another repository

### The evidence

Your GitHub profile now contains real activity: issues filed, pull requests merged, code reviewed, and capstone evidence prepared for a real repository. This is not a certificate. It is a commit history.

---

## 2. Your New Skills Inventory

The following table maps what you learned to where it applies beyond this workshop. Every skill transfers directly to real-world development.

| Skill | Where you learned it | Where it applies |
|---|---|---|
| Repository navigation | Chapters 2-3 | Every GitHub project, every job that uses GitHub |
| Issue tracking | Chapter 5 | Bug reports, feature requests, project management |
| Pull request workflow | Chapters 6, 15 | Code contribution at any company or open source project |
| Merge conflict resolution | Chapter 7 | Any team project with multiple contributors |
| Git fundamentals | Chapters 13-14 | Every software project that uses version control |
| VS Code proficiency | Chapters 11-12 | Daily development work in any language |
| Code review | Chapter 15 | Peer review, quality assurance, team collaboration |
| Fork workflow | Chapter 18 | Open source contribution, cross-team collaboration |
| AI-assisted development | Chapters 16, 19-20 | GitHub Copilot, AI agents, and future AI tools |
| Accessibility awareness | Entire workshop | Building inclusive software, WCAG compliance |

### Skills you may not have noticed

- **Reading documentation:** You navigated technical guides, followed step-by-step instructions, and troubleshot problems using written references. This is the most important developer skill.
- **Asking for help effectively:** You posted on issues with context, error messages, and what you tried. This is how experienced developers communicate.
- **Learning tools by doing:** You did not read a manual cover to cover. You tried things, hit problems, and figured them out. This is how real tool learning works.

---

## 3. Building Your Developer Portfolio

> **See also:** [Appendix X: Resources](appendix-x-resources.md) has links to every tool and resource mentioned in this course.

Your GitHub profile is your portfolio. Here is how to make what you built visible.

### Pin your best repositories

1. Go to [github.com/settings/profile](https://github.com/settings/profile).
2. Scroll to "Pinned repositories."
3. Pin the repositories that show your best work. Consider:
   - Your fork of the accessibility-agents repository (shows open source contribution)
   - Any personal projects you create after the workshop

### Write a profile README

Your profile README is the first thing people see when they visit your GitHub profile. Create a repository with the same name as your username (e.g., `your-username/your-username`) and add a `README.md`:

```markdown
# Hi, I am [Your Name]

I am a developer focused on [your interests].

## Recent work

- Prepared a capstone contribution for Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another repository
- Completed the Git Going with GitHub workshop

## What I am learning

- [List technologies or topics you are exploring]
```

### Keep your contribution graph active

The green squares on your GitHub profile show when you made contributions. Even small actions count: filing issues, opening PRs, making commits, and reviewing code. Consistency matters more than volume.

### Learning Cards: Building Your Developer Portfolio

**Screen reader users:**

- Navigate to your profile settings at github.com/settings/profile -- the "Pinned repositories" section is a group of checkboxes; Tab through and press Space to pin or unpin
- Your profile README repository must match your username exactly (case-sensitive) -- screen readers will read the rendered README as regular page content when visitors navigate your profile
- The contribution graph is announced as a table or grid; arrow keys move between day cells, each announcing the date and contribution count

**Low-vision users:**

- Pinned repositories appear as cards below your avatar -- at high zoom the 2x3 grid may reflow to a single column, which is easier to scan
- The profile README renders with your current GitHub theme -- test yours in both light and dark modes to confirm text and images remain readable
- Contribution graph squares use green intensity to show activity levels; enable high-contrast mode if the shading differences are hard to distinguish

**Sighted users:**

- Pinned repos appear in a 2x3 grid directly below your bio -- visitors see them immediately, so choose repos that showcase your best work
- Your profile README renders above the pinned repos section -- keep it concise and scannable with headings and bullet points
- The contribution graph shows a full year of activity; consistent small green squares look better to visitors than occasional intense bursts

---

## 4. Continued Learning Roadmap

> **See also:** [Appendix Z: GitHub Skills](appendix-z-github-skills.md) has the complete catalog of recommended GitHub Skills courses.

The workshop taught you the fundamentals. Here is where to go deeper in each area.

### Git and version control

- [Pro Git book](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) -- Free, comprehensive, and the official Git resource. Start with chapters 2 and 3.
- [Appendix E: Advanced Git](appendix-e-advanced-git.md) -- Rebasing, cherry-picking, stashing, and other techniques you will need eventually.

### GitHub platform

- [GitHub Docs](https://docs.github.com) -- The official documentation covers everything. Bookmark it.
- [GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com) -- Free, interactive courses that teach by doing (see Section 5 below).
- [GitHub Blog](https://github.blog) -- Stay current with new features and best practices.

### VS Code

- [VS Code documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs) -- Complete reference for settings, keybindings, and extensions.
- [VS Code accessibility documentation](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/accessibility) -- Deep dive into screen reader support, high contrast, and keyboard navigation.

### Accessibility

- [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/) -- The quick reference version is the most practical.
- [Appendix M: Accessibility Standards](appendix-m-accessibility-standards.md) -- Workshop reference for WCAG criteria used in this course.
- [WebAIM](https://webaim.org) -- Practical accessibility resources, training, and tools.
- [Deque University](https://dequeuniversity.com) -- Free and paid courses on web accessibility.

### AI-assisted development

- [GitHub Copilot documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot) -- Official docs for Copilot features, configuration, and best practices.
- [Appendix K: Copilot Reference](appendix-k-copilot-reference.md) -- Workshop quick-reference card.
- [Appendix L: Agents Reference](appendix-l-agents-reference.md) -- Full accessibility agents roster and command reference.

### Programming languages

Choose based on your interests:

| Interest | Language to learn | Where to start |
|---|---|---|
| Web development | HTML, CSS, JavaScript | [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org) |
| Automation and scripting | Python | [Python.org tutorial](https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/) |
| Desktop applications | Python (with wxPython or Tkinter) | [wxPython documentation](https://docs.wxpython.org) |
| Mobile development | Swift (iOS) or Kotlin (Android) | Platform-specific developer docs |

---

## 5. GitHub Skills Courses to Try Next

[GitHub Skills](https://skills.github.com) offers free, interactive courses that run inside GitHub repositories. Each course creates a repository in your account with step-by-step instructions and automated feedback -- the same model we used in this workshop.

### Recommended next courses

| Course | What you will learn | How it connects to this workshop |
|---|---|---|
| [Introduction to GitHub](https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-github) | Repository basics, branches, commits, PRs | Review and reinforce Day 1 skills |
| [Communicate using Markdown](https://github.com/skills/communicate-using-markdown) | Markdown syntax, formatting, links, images | Write better issues, PRs, and documentation |
| [Review pull requests](https://github.com/skills/review-pull-requests) | Review workflow, inline comments, suggestions | Deepen the code review skills from Chapter 15 |
| [Resolve merge conflicts](https://github.com/skills/resolve-merge-conflicts) | Conflict detection, resolution strategies | Practice what you learned in Chapter 7 |
| [Getting Started with GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/skills/getting-started-with-github-copilot) | Copilot suggestions, chat, and prompting | Extend Chapter 16 with hands-on Copilot practice |
| [Code with Copilot](https://github.com/skills/code-with-copilot) | Multi-file editing, code review with Copilot | Build on the AI-assisted workflow from Day 2 |

### How to start a course

1. Go to [skills.github.com](https://skills.github.com).
2. Find a course and click its title.
3. Click **Start course** (this creates a repository in your account).
4. Follow the instructions in the repository's README.

Each course takes 15 to 60 minutes.

---

## 6. Staying Connected

### Community Access

- [Community Access on GitHub](https://github.com/Community-Access) -- The organization behind this workshop. Watch the repositories for updates.
- For post-workshop questions, troubleshooting, and alumni conversation, use the open support hub: [Community-Access/support](https://github.com/Community-Access/support).

### Open source contribution

The capstone was your first contribution. Here is how to make more:

1. **Start with projects you use.** If you use a tool or library and find a bug or missing documentation, that is your first issue.
2. **Look for "good first issue" labels.** Many projects label issues that are suitable for new contributors.
3. **Documentation counts.** Fixing typos, improving instructions, and adding examples are valuable contributions. Do not underestimate them.
4. **The fork workflow scales.** The same fork, branch, commit, push, PR workflow from [Chapter 18](18-fork-and-contribute.md) works for every GitHub project.

### Accessibility community

- [GitHub Accessibility documentation](https://accessibility.github.com) -- Official accessibility guides for GitHub's interface.
- [WebAIM mailing list](https://webaim.org/discussion/) -- Active discussion forum for web accessibility practitioners.
- [A11y Project](https://www.a11yproject.com) -- Community-driven accessibility resources and checklist.

---

## 7. Contributing Back to This Workshop

This workshop is open source. If you found something confusing, incorrect, or missing, you can fix it.

### Types of contributions we value

| Contribution | How to do it |
|---|---|
| Fix a typo or broken link | Open a PR directly |
| Clarify confusing instructions | File an issue describing what confused you, then open a PR |
| Add a screen reader tip | File an issue with the tip and the chapter it belongs in |
| Report an accessibility barrier | File an issue with the heading "Accessibility barrier" |
| Suggest a new topic | File an issue with the heading "Content suggestion" |

### The contribution workflow

1. Fork the [git-going-with-github](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github) repository.
2. Clone your fork, create a branch, make your edit.
3. Open a PR with a clear title and description.
4. Mention the chapter number and section in your PR.

You have already practiced every step of this workflow. This is the real thing.

### Learning Cards: Contributing Back to This Workshop

**Screen reader users:**

- The contribution workflow here is identical to Chapter 18 (Fork and Contribute) -- fork, clone, branch, edit, push, PR; use the same keyboard and screen reader patterns you already practiced
- When filing an issue, include the chapter number and section heading in the title so maintainers can locate the problem with heading navigation
- After opening a PR, listen for the automated check results in the PR timeline -- each check is announced as a link with its pass/fail status

**Low-vision users:**

- The contribution types table above maps each kind of contribution to its workflow -- zoom in on the "How to do it" column for the quickest path
- When editing documentation in your fork, use VS Code's Markdown Preview (`Ctrl+Shift+V`) at your preferred zoom level to verify formatting before pushing
- PR descriptions render as Markdown on GitHub -- use headings and lists so reviewers can scan your changes at any zoom level

**Sighted users:**

- The simplest contribution is fixing a typo -- fork the repo, edit the file directly on GitHub.com, and open a PR in under two minutes
- Reference the chapter number and section in your PR title (e.g., "Fix broken link in Ch07 Section 3") so maintainers can review quickly
- Check the repository's open issues for items labeled "good first issue" or "help wanted" to find contributions the maintainers are actively seeking

---

## If You Get Stuck After the Workshop

Before you open a new browser tab and search the whole internet, use the workshop support path you already practiced. Start with the [Course Guide](course-guide.md) when you need the map, the [Challenge Hub](CHALLENGES.md) when you need the challenge-by-challenge checklist, and [Get Going with GitHub](get-going.md) when you need the onboarding path again. These pages are not separate podcast episodes because they are navigation aids, but this closing chapter is the right place to name them.

If you need human help, use the Community Access support hub. Include what you tried, what happened, what you expected, your operating system, and the screen reader or access tools you are using. That is the same evidence habit you practiced in issues and pull requests.

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| Forgot how to do something from the workshop | Search the [course guide](course-guide.md) by topic. Every major skill links to the chapter and appendix that covers it. |
| Git error you have not seen before | Copy the exact error text and search for it. [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) and Stack Overflow's [git tag](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/git) cover nearly every scenario. |
| VS Code extension not working | Check the extension's page in the marketplace for known issues. Try disabling and re-enabling it. |
| Want to contribute but do not know where to start | Search for `good first issue` labels on projects that interest you. See [Section 4: Continued Learning Roadmap](#4-continued-learning-roadmap). |
| Need help from the community | Post in [Support Hub Discussions](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/discussions) or file a [support issue](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/issues). |

## 8. Final Words

Two days ago, GitHub was new. Git was a mystery. The terminal was unfamiliar. Now you have filed issues, opened pull requests, resolved conflicts, reviewed code, and contributed to a real open source project.

The tools are yours now. The workflow is yours. The confidence is yours.

Every expert started exactly where you are standing. The difference between a beginner and an experienced developer is not talent -- it is reps. You just finished your first set.

Keep committing.

[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we get into the design challenge, what should learners already have in place?

[ALEX]
A few practical things. First, you should already know how to work with GitHub issues at a basic level. Second, you need a repository where you can create or edit files, usually your fork or your own repo. Third, it really helps to use an editor with YAML syntax highlighting, such as VS Code.

[JAMIE]
And some things are recommended but not strictly required, right?

[ALEX]
Right. Familiarity with GitHub Copilot can help if you want to generate variations, but it's optional. Basic terminal comfort is useful, though you can also use the GitHub web editor or github.dev. And if you already filled out the workshop registration template earlier in this course, that template becomes a learning example now.

[ALEX]
Plan roughly two to two and a half hours if you do the exercises and some YAML troubleshooting.

The learning pattern for this challenge is analyze, remix, create, and test.
